extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy and law
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Hobbesian doctrines on natural and civil liberty, the rights and obligations of subjects, and the constitution, limits, and liabilities of bodies politique (corporate/representative assemblies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of liberty (natural liberty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty is not the liberty of voice or of a particular appetite, but that of the man who finds no stop in doing what he has the will, desire, or inclination to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that 'freewill' refers to the liberty of the person (ability to act without external impediment), not a metaphysical freedom of the will; liberty consists in absence of external constraint preventing an intended action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear and liberty consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions done for fear (e.g., throwing goods into the sea for fear the ship sinks, paying a debt for fear of imprisonment) are nevertheless voluntary and may be refused; thus fear and liberty are consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: throwing goods away under fear is still a free action because the agent may refuse; many commonwealth actions done for fear of the law remain actions of a free person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty and necessity consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary actions proceed from liberty (the will) yet also proceed from causes tracing to necessity; seeing the causal chain (ultimately to God) would make all voluntary acts appear necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy of water obliged to descend by a channel: actions can be both voluntary and caused; reconciles liberty with causal necessity in human actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil laws as artificial bonds/covenants
rubrics_metrics.description: Men create an 'artificial man' (commonwealth) and 'artificial chains' (civil laws) by mutual covenants fastening obligations to the sovereign's commands and to the subjects' ears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These bonds are weak in themselves but are made to hold by danger (sanctions) rather than intrinsic difficulty of breaking them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of subjects consists in liberty from covenants (praetermitted areas)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject's liberty lies only in those things which the sovereign has omitted to regulate — e.g., liberty to buy and sell, choose abode, diet, trade, instruct children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes subject liberty from absence of sovereignty: liberty is confined to what the sovereign leaves unregulated; neither corporeal freedom nor exemption from laws in general are what subjects claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject liberty compatible with sovereign's unlimited power
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject liberty does not abolish or limit sovereign power (including power of life and death); acts of the sovereign are not unjust to subjects because subjects are the authors of sovereign acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jeptha's daughter, David and Uriah — a sovereign may lawfully put a subject to death and not be unjust to the subject, though it may be against the law of Nature and thus an offense against God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty praised by ancients is liberty of commonwealths not private men
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient notions of 'liberty' (Greeks/Romans) refer to the freedom of a commonwealth (state) to act, not to individual private liberty to resist a representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Athenians and Romans were 'free' as commonwealths; individual liberty within popular states differs from private men under monarchy; confusion of these concepts breeds sedition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring the liberty of the subject (by words or intention of submission)
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine what liberties are yielded on making a commonwealth, one must examine the express words of submission ('I authorise all his actions') or the intention/end of the covenant (peace and defense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obligations and liberties follow either from explicit language of authorization or from the end (safety/protection) for which sovereignty was instituted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects have liberty to defend their own bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Covenants that require a person not to defend his own body are void; every subject retains a right to self-defense that cannot be transferred away by covenant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sovereign commanded a man to kill, wound, or starve himself, he may disobey; likewise a subject is not obliged to confess a crime absent assurance of pardon (can't be bound to self-accusation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Not bound to hurt themselves (self-harm exemption)
rubrics_metrics.description: The words of consent to sovereign power ('I authorise all his actions') do not bind one to kill oneself or another at the sovereign's command; such obligations are beyond mere words and depend on intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between allowing the sovereign to kill you ('Kill me, or my fellow, if you please') and promising to kill oneself; refusal to obey is justified when obedience would not serve the end for which sovereignty was instituted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not obliged to warfare unless voluntarily undertaken
rubrics_metrics.description: A man commanded as a soldier may in some cases refuse (e.g., substitute a sufficient soldier) and natural timorousness is allowed; but enlistment or taking impress money removes such excuse and imposes obligation to fight and not flee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Desertion out of fear is dishonourable though not always unjust; when defense requires all able, everyone is obliged to serve, else the institution of commonwealth fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot lawfully resist sovereign to defend another (with limited exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: No man has liberty to resist the sword of the commonwealth to defend another person, because that would remove the means of protection. Exception: if many have already resisted the sovereign unjustly and expect death, they may defend themselves collectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If many have already rebelled, subsequent bearing of arms to defend their persons may not be unjust; an offer of pardon removes the plea of self-defense and makes continued resistance unlawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatest liberty depends on silence of the law
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects enjoy liberty in areas where the sovereign has prescribed no rule; such liberties vary by place and time according to sovereign discretion (examples: forcible entry, polygamy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liberties change if sovereign or legislature enacts statutes (e.g., a statute forbade forcible entry that was formerly allowed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject's right to sue when sovereign acts by force of former law
rubrics_metrics.description: If the sovereign demands something by the force of a former law (not by virtue of sovereign power), the subject has liberty to sue for his right before judges appointed by the sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a suit is not contrary to the sovereign's will because the sovereign is invoking a law rather than sovereign prerogative; but actions taken by the sovereign as sovereign (virtue of power) are not legally actionable by subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grants of liberty void if incompatible with sovereign's ability to provide safety
rubrics_metrics.description: If the sovereign grants a liberty that disables his ability to ensure safety (e.g., powers necessary to exercise sovereignty), the grant is void unless he renounces/transfers sovereignty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powers necessary to sovereignty include war/peace, judicature, appointment of officers, levying money; consequences that contradict the sovereign's will are not to be inferred from grants unless plainly expressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects absolved when sovereign fails to protect (scope of obligation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obedience lasts only so long as the sovereign retains the power to protect; if the sovereign loses that capacity (violent death, war, or internal collapse), subjects revert to natural liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereignty is the soul of the commonwealth; when it departs, members no longer receive motion from it and natural right to self-protection resumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captivity: acceptance of conditions binds subject to victor
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person taken prisoner accepts terms that give him life and corporal liberty on condition of subjection to the victor, he has liberty to accept and, having accepted, becomes subject to the victor; but if merely detained without consent, escape is permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between voluntary acceptance of terms (creates obligation) and detention/ imprisonment where no covenant is formed (escape justified).

rubrics_metrics.name: If sovereign abdicates or dies without heir, subjects return to natural liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Should a monarch relinquish sovereignty for himself and his heirs, or die without known heir or declaration, subjects return to absolute natural liberty because there is no successor to institute subjection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relinquishment or absence of heir dissolves the chain of subjection; natural ties (kin) do not on their own create sovereignty without the sovereign's will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banishment frees subject during exile; travel does not
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject banished is not a subject during banishment; a person sent on a message or with leave to travel remains a subject (though under other sovereigns' laws while in their dominions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entry into another dominion subjects one to that dominion's laws unless privileged by amity or special license.

rubrics_metrics.name: If sovereign renders himself subject to another, effect on subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: If a monarch, conquered by war, renders himself subject to the victor, his subjects become delivered from former obligation and become obliged to the victor; if the monarch is merely a prisoner without liberty, his right may remain and subjects may still be obliged to magistrates acting in his name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between voluntary cession (transfers obligation) and mere captivity where sovereign's right persists and administration continues under previously appointed magistrates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and taxonomy of systemes (bodies, regular/irregular)
rubrics_metrics.description: Systemes are any numbers of men joined in one interest or business; regular systems have a constituted representative, irregular ones do not; regular systems may be absolute/independent (commonwealths) or dependent (subject to higher sovereign); private vs political systems and lawful vs unlawful distinctions explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irregular lawful concourses (markets, shows) are permissible; irregular or private systems with evil intent or large unknown numbers are unlawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of representative in bodies politique is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: In every body politique the power of its representative is limited; limits are prescribed by the sovereign and derived from letters (writ) or the laws of the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting a body absolute representative power to all intents is effectively abandoning governance over that portion of the commonwealth and therefore not to be presumed without explicit words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of subordinate bodies by letters patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Subordinate bodies' powers and limits should be taken from their letters or commissions from the sovereign, often formalized by letters patent sealed to be read publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because subordinate bodies’ businesses, times, and places vary, written, sealed documentation is necessary to fix limitations and communicate authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits supplied by ordinary laws where letters silent
rubrics_metrics.description: When letters patent are silent or incomplete, ordinary common laws determine what the representative may lawfully do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary laws common to all subjects fill gaps in commissions and set the bounds of a representative's lawful action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where representative is one man, unwarranted acts are his personal acts only
rubrics_metrics.description: If a body's representative is a single man, anything he does beyond his letters or the laws is his own act and not the act of the body or its members; acts within letters/laws are acts of every member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative's acts outside authority do not bind members; within authority, the representative acts as the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where representative is an assembly, only consenting members are bound
rubrics_metrics.description: If the representative is an assembly, decrees not warranted by letters/laws are the act of the assembly and of every one who voted for the decree, but not of dissenters or absentees (except by proxy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemblies are capable of corporate punishment (dissolution, forfeiture of letters) but individual non-voters are innocent of unwarranted acts; majority vote makes it the act of the assembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debt liability when representative is one man
rubrics_metrics.description: If the representative (one man) borrows money from a stranger, the debt is the representative's personal obligation and the members are not liable, since lending strangers can only regard the representative as debtor unless letters authorize otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarly, if he comes into debt by contract or mulct (fine), the liability is his alone, not the members'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debt liability when representative is an assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: When the representative is an assembly, only those who assented (voted) to the borrowing or contract are responsible for the debt or mulct; the author of the borrowing is obliged even if one person pays the whole debt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voting to borrow engages the voter's personal obligation for the liability created by the assembly's act.

rubrics_metrics.name: If debt is to one of the assembly, the body only is obliged
rubrics_metrics.description: If the debt is owed to one of the assembly members, the assembly alone is obliged to pay out of their common stock; the lender-member cannot demand payment from any particular man but only from the common treasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If common treasure fails, the lender has remedy only against himself for lending foolishly, not against particular members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to protest against decrees of subordinate bodies (not against sovereign)
rubrics_metrics.description: In subordinate bodies politque it is sometimes lawful and expedient for a member to publicly protest and register dissent against decrees; protesting against a sovereign assembly, however, denies sovereignty and is not permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protest protects members from being held liable for acts they did not assent to in subordinate bodies; protest in sovereign assembly removes recognition of sovereign authority and thus is impermissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bodies politique for provinces/colonies/towns: limits on jurisdiction and obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemblies governing provinces/colonies/towns have authority limited by commission and cannot execute power outside their colony (e.g., seize persons or goods beyond colony bounds); debts or unlawful acts are the act of those who assented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a member is injured by such a body, cognisance of his cause belongs to the sovereign or judges appointed by sovereign, not to the body itself; local assemblies may impose mulcts but cannot execute them beyond their territorial jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bodies for ordering trade and incorporation as monopolies
rubrics_metrics.description: A body politique incorporated to order foreign traffic (company of merchants) often functions as a double monopoly (sole buyer at home, sole seller abroad), profitable to adventurers but disadvantageous to the people at home and to foreigners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such corporations raise prices at home and depress prices abroad to the detriment of non-members; the end of incorporation is particular gain of adventurers, so participants should be included in governance and acquainted with accounts.
